questions.stem: The tragedy of the commons describes a situation in which:
options: a resource owned by one person is protected because the owner bears all the costs
a community agrees on rules that keep a shared resource in good condition
individuals acting in their own interest overuse a shared resource until it is degraded
a government sells a public resource to a private owner, who then overuses it for profit
questions.explanation: When a resource is open to all, each user gains the full benefit of taking more but shares the cost of damage with everyone, so the resource tends to be overused. Community rules that conserve the resource are a way of avoiding the tragedy, not the tragedy itself.

questions.stem: Who popularised the idea of the tragedy of the commons in a 1968 essay in the journal Science?
options: Rachel Carson
Gro Harlem Brundtland
Charles Darwin
Garrett Hardin
questions.explanation: Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay used the example of herders grazing a shared pasture. Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring about pesticides, and Brundtland chaired the commission that defined sustainable development.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best example of a commons resource?
options: Fish stocks in the open ocean beyond any one country's control
Timber growing in a privately owned and securely fenced plantation
Water stored in a household rainwater tank on a farm
Minerals under land leased to a single mining company
questions.explanation: A commons is open to many users and hard to exclude people from, such as high-seas fisheries or the atmosphere. Privately owned plantations, tanks and leased minerals have a single owner who controls access.

questions.stem: Ten farmers share a groundwater aquifer. Each farmer gains the full profit from pumping extra water, but the falling water table affects all ten. Why does this tend to lead to overuse?
options: Groundwater is renewed faster than it can be pumped, so there is no real cost
The government owns the aquifer, so the farmers have no incentive to pump water
Each farmer gets all the benefit of extra pumping but bears only a share of the cost
Each farmer bears all the cost of extra pumping but gets only a share of the benefit
questions.explanation: The private benefit of pumping goes to the individual, while the cost of a lower water table is spread across all users, so each has an incentive to take more. This mismatch drives the tragedy of the commons.

questions.stem: Which management approach would most directly avoid a tragedy of the commons in a shared rock lobster fishery?
options: Subsidising bigger boats so fishers can travel to distant grounds
Removing size limits so that fishers can keep every lobster caught
Setting a total allowable catch divided into individual quotas
Allowing unlimited licences so that every fisher can compete freely
questions.explanation: A total allowable catch caps the harvest at a sustainable level, and individual quotas give each fisher a secure share, removing the race to fish. Unlimited licences, subsidies and no size limits all increase fishing pressure.

questions.stem: Why is the atmosphere often described as a global commons?
options: Everyone can release gases into it, and no single owner controls its use
It is owned by the United Nations, which sets the emission limits for every country
Only countries that produce oil are able to release gases into it
Gases released into it stay above the country that emitted them
questions.explanation: Any person or country can emit into the atmosphere, and the effects, such as climate change, are shared globally. No body owns it, which is why international agreements are needed to manage emissions.

questions.stem: Intergenerational equity means that:
options: older people living today should always have priority access to resources over younger people
each generation should use up resources quickly before they are lost to others
the present generation should leave future generations an environment at least as healthy as now
resources should be shared fairly among people of different countries living today
questions.explanation: Intergenerational equity is fairness between generations: today's use should not reduce the health, diversity and productivity of the environment for those who follow. Fairness among people alive today is intragenerational equity.

questions.stem: Intragenerational equity is concerned with fairness:
options: among governments competing for international trade
among people of the present generation, including social equity
between the present generation and the generations not yet born
between humans and all other species in an ecosystem
questions.explanation: Intragenerational equity means sharing the benefits and costs of resource use fairly among people alive now, within and between communities and countries. Fairness to future generations is intergenerational equity.

questions.stem: A city's air pollution is worst in low-income suburbs beside a highway, while wealthier suburbs enjoy clean air. Which ESD principle is most clearly not being met?
options: Intragenerational equity
Intergenerational equity
Efficiency of resource use
The user pays principle
questions.explanation: The costs of pollution fall unfairly on one group of people living today, which breaches intragenerational (social) equity. Intergenerational equity concerns fairness to future generations.

questions.stem: A government decides not to drain an old-growth peat swamp for farmland so that the swamp's carbon store and species remain for people in 100 years. Which principle does this mainly reflect?
options: Intragenerational equity
The user pays principle
Social licence to operate
Intergenerational equity
questions.explanation: Keeping the swamp intact protects its values for future generations, which is intergenerational equity. Intragenerational equity concerns fair sharing among people alive now.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the precautionary principle?
options: A development should always go ahead unless science proves beyond doubt that it causes serious harm
Action to protect the environment should wait until the science is completely certain
Developers must pay for any damage they cause once it has been measured and proven
Lack of full scientific certainty should not delay action to prevent serious or irreversible damage
questions.explanation: Where there is a threat of serious or irreversible environmental damage, uncertainty is not a reason to postpone preventive measures. Requiring proof of harm before acting is the opposite approach, and paying for proven damage is the polluter pays principle.

questions.stem: A company proposes to release a genetically modified bacterium to clean up an oil spill. Laboratory trials look promising, but its effects on marine food webs are unknown. Which response best applies the precautionary principle?
options: Release it immediately, since no evidence yet shows it harms marine food webs
Release it and then monitor, paying compensation later if harm is detected
Ban all oil spill clean-up methods until the science of every one is certain
Delay release until field trials in contained sites show the risks are acceptable
questions.explanation: With unknown but potentially serious effects, the precautionary approach is to act cautiously, gathering evidence in controlled conditions before release. Treating no evidence of harm as evidence of safety reverses the principle, while banning every method is not proportionate.

questions.stem: The precautionary principle is often described as anticipatory. What does this mean?
options: It aims to transfer the cost of harm from the polluter to taxpayers
It aims to foresee and prevent harm rather than repair it afterwards
It aims to repair environmental damage as soon as it has occurred
It aims to wait until the full costs of harm have been calculated
questions.explanation: Anticipatory means acting ahead of time: identifying likely harm and preventing it, because some damage, such as extinction, cannot be undone. Repair after the event is a reactive approach.

questions.stem: Which action best shows the ESD principle of conserving biodiversity and ecological integrity?
options: Planting a single fast-growing exotic tree species across the whole of a cleared hillside
Draining a wetland to create a lake that suits recreational boating
Replacing a native grassland with irrigated pasture for higher production
Retaining corridors of native vegetation that link patches of habitat on a farm
questions.explanation: Habitat corridors maintain the variety of species and the ecological processes that connect populations. Monocultures, drainage and conversion to pasture reduce biodiversity and alter natural processes.

questions.stem: Ecological integrity refers to an ecosystem that:
options: has been cleared and then replanted so that it looks the same as it did before clearing
produces the greatest possible yield of timber or food each year
contains as many introduced species as possible to raise diversity
keeps its natural structure, species and processes and can recover from disturbance
questions.explanation: An ecosystem with integrity has its characteristic species, structure and processes, such as nutrient cycling, and is resilient to disturbance. High yield or an appearance of naturalness does not mean these are intact.

questions.stem: Households paying for water by the kilolitre used, rather than a flat fee, is an example of:
options: the precautionary principle
a social licence to operate
the user pays principle
intergenerational equity
questions.explanation: User pays prices a natural resource so that those who use more pay more, encouraging careful use. The precautionary principle concerns acting under scientific uncertainty.

questions.stem: Why does pricing environmental values and natural resources support ESD?
options: A price guarantees that a resource can never be used up or degraded
A price removes the need for any further government regulation of the resource
A price makes the resource free for future generations to use later
A price makes users weigh the true value of a resource, discouraging waste
questions.explanation: When a resource is free, it tends to be overused; pricing signals its value and encourages efficient use. Pricing alone does not guarantee conservation, so regulation is still needed.

questions.stem: A factory redesigns its process so that it produces the same output with 25% less water and energy. Which ESD principle is this?
options: Intragenerational equity
The precautionary principle
Conservation of biodiversity
Efficiency of resource use
questions.explanation: Producing the same output with fewer resources is improved efficiency of resource use. It reduces pressure on resources but does not directly address fairness or uncertainty.

questions.stem: A wind farm would cut carbon emissions for decades, but its turbines would be built on the only known breeding site of a threatened eagle. Which two ESD principles are in tension?
options: Efficiency of resource use and social licence to operate
Intergenerational equity and conservation of biodiversity
The user pays principle and efficiency of resource use
Intragenerational equity and the user pays principle
questions.explanation: Cutting emissions protects the climate for future generations (intergenerational equity), but destroying the breeding site threatens biodiversity. ESD requires decision makers to weigh such conflicts rather than apply one principle alone.

questions.stem: A council plans to fund new stormwater wetlands by raising rates equally on all households, including pensioners who use little water. A critic says a charge based on water use would be fairer. Which principles does the critic appeal to?
options: Intergenerational equity and biodiversity
Social licence and the precautionary principle
User pays and intragenerational equity
Precautionary principle and efficiency
questions.explanation: Charging by use applies the user pays principle, and the concern for low-income pensioners reflects fairness among people now, which is intragenerational equity. Neither uncertainty nor future generations is the issue raised.

questions.stem: Ecologically sustainable development is best described as development that:
options: meets present needs while maintaining ecological processes for the future
maximises economic growth in the short term regardless of environmental cost
stops all use of natural resources so that ecosystems remain untouched
protects the environment only where this does not reduce company profits
questions.explanation: ESD aims to improve quality of life now and in the future by using resources in ways that keep the ecological processes on which life depends. It is not a ban on resource use, nor growth at any cost.

questions.stem: A forestry company plans to clear-fell old-growth forest to export woodchips. Which change to the plan would best bring it into line with ESD principles?
options: Clear-fell the old-growth forest and plant a single exotic species to replace the old trees
Clear-fell the old-growth forest but donate a share of the woodchip profits to local charity
Harvest selectively from regrowth forest and protect old-growth stands and streamside reserves
Clear-fell the old-growth forest faster so that the profits arrive sooner for the community
questions.explanation: Protecting old-growth and streamside areas conserves biodiversity and ecological integrity, and harvesting regrowth keeps the resource available for future generations. Donations or faster harvesting do not address the loss of irreplaceable habitat.

questions.stem: How many Sustainable Development Goals did the United Nations adopt in 2015?
questions.explanation: UN member states adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. They replaced the eight Millennium Development Goals.

questions.stem: By which year are the UN Sustainable Development Goals intended to be achieved?
questions.explanation: The goals form the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted in 2015 with a target year of 2030.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the scope of the UN Sustainable Development Goals?
options: They deal only with protecting wildlife and natural areas in developing countries
They set legally binding emission limits that every member country must meet by law
They focus only on economic growth, leaving environmental issues to each nation
They link ending poverty and inequality with protecting the environment and climate
questions.explanation: The goals cover social, economic and environmental aims together, such as no poverty, clean water, climate action and life below water. They are not a legally binding treaty with fixed national limits.

questions.stem: A Tasmanian council project restores seagrass beds and reduces stormwater pollution in an estuary. Which Sustainable Development Goal theme does this most directly support?
options: Quality education
Gender equality
Zero hunger
Life below water
questions.explanation: Restoring seagrass and cutting pollution protect marine and coastal ecosystems, which is the focus of the goal on life below water. The other goals address education, equality and food security.

questions.stem: Why might pursuing one Sustainable Development Goal work against another?
options: Expanding farmland to end hunger can clear habitat and reduce life on land
Each goal applies only to a single country, so they never overlap at all
The goals are ranked, so achieving the first one cancels all the others
Environmental goals can only be met once all economic goals are achieved
questions.explanation: The goals interact: producing more food can mean clearing land, which harms biodiversity. Good planning seeks solutions, such as higher yields on existing farmland, that advance several goals together.

questions.stem: A social licence to operate is best described as:
options: a formal permit issued by government after an environmental assessment
a contract signed between a developer and the local council before work
a fee paid by a company to the community for the right to use resources
an informal acceptance or approval of a development by the community
questions.explanation: A social licence is the ongoing, informal acceptance of a project by the community and stakeholders. It is not a legal document, so a project can hold all its government permits and still lack a social licence.

questions.stem: A mining company has all the government approvals it needs, but local residents stage protests and boycott the company. What does this situation show?
options: The company has met every principle of sustainable development
A social licence is granted automatically with a government permit
Legal approval does not guarantee a social licence to operate
The residents have cancelled the company's government permits
questions.explanation: Legal permits and community acceptance are separate. A company can be lawfully approved yet lose community support, which can delay projects, damage reputation and lead governments to review conditions.

questions.stem: Which action is most likely to help a salmon farming company build a social licence to operate in a coastal community?
options: Publishing its water quality monitoring openly and acting on community concerns
Keeping its environmental monitoring data confidential to protect its business interests
Expanding its pens quickly before the community has a chance to comment
Relying only on its government licence when residents raise concerns
questions.explanation: Transparency, genuine consultation and responsiveness build trust and community acceptance. Secrecy, rushing expansion or relying only on legal approval tend to erode a social licence.

questions.stem: Why can a social licence to operate be lost even after a project has started?
options: It is cancelled by a court whenever any member of the community lodges a complaint
It applies only during construction and ends when the project begins operating
It depends on continuing community trust, which can fall if impacts or behaviour change
It expires automatically after a fixed term written into the government permit
questions.explanation: Because a social licence rests on ongoing trust rather than a legal document, it can be withdrawn if a company causes unexpected harm, breaks promises or ignores concerns. It has no fixed term and is not issued by a court.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder group grants or withholds a social licence to operate?
options: The company's board of directors and its shareholders alone
The government department that issues environmental permits
An international court that hears environmental disputes
The community and other stakeholders affected by the project
questions.explanation: A social licence comes from the community and stakeholders who are affected by, or interested in, a project. Government grants legal permits, which are a separate matter.

questions.stem: A proposal would dam a wild river for hydro-electricity, supplying renewable power to the state but flooding a gorge with rare plants and high scenic value. A group argues that the gorge's loss cannot be reversed. Which ESD principle best supports their position?
options: The user pays principle, because electricity users would pay for power
Efficiency of resource use, because hydro-electricity wastes less water
Intragenerational equity, because power would be shared fairly today
The precautionary principle, because the damage would be irreversible
questions.explanation: When damage would be serious and irreversible, the precautionary principle weighs against proceeding without strong justification, and intergenerational equity also applies. The other principles do not address the permanence of the loss.

questions.stem: A fishery sets catch limits each year based on scientific surveys of fish stocks, and reduces limits when surveys are uncertain. Which ESD principles does this best show?
options: Efficiency of resource use and social licence to operate
Pricing environmental values and intragenerational equity
Intergenerational equity and the precautionary principle
Intragenerational equity and the user pays principle
questions.explanation: Science-based limits keep the stock available for future fishers (intergenerational equity), and lowering limits under uncertainty is precautionary. The scenario says nothing about pricing or fairness among current users.

questions.stem: Why is a growing human population a challenge for ecologically sustainable development?
options: It guarantees intergenerational equity because more people will exist in the future
It has no effect on resource use because technology always keeps pace with demand
It increases demand for food, water, energy and land, placing more pressure on ecosystems
It reduces the overall demand for resources because more people can share the existing supply
questions.explanation: More people need more resources and produce more waste, increasing pressure on ecosystems and making it harder to keep resources available for the future. Technology can improve efficiency but does not automatically offset rising demand.

questions.stem: A government compares two plans for a coastal town. Plan X builds a seawall that protects houses now but causes beaches downstream to erode. Plan Y restores dunes and plants vegetation, protecting houses more slowly but keeping beaches. Which statement best evaluates them against ESD?
options: Neither plan relates to ESD because coastal protection is only an engineering issue
Plan Y better conserves ecological integrity, though it may take longer to protect homes
Plan X better conserves ecological integrity, because it protects houses straight away
Both plans equally meet ESD principles because both aim to protect the town's houses
questions.explanation: Dune restoration works with natural processes and keeps beach ecosystems, conserving ecological integrity for the future. The seawall offers faster protection but transfers erosion elsewhere, so the plans differ in how well they meet ESD.
